rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At resurrection every creature is within another's sight, yet each is absorbed in himself and does not speak to or ask relatives.
rows.anchor: وليس في القيامة مخلوق إلا وهو نصب عين صاحبه من الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: People recognize one another for an hour, then cease recognizing one another.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: يتعارفون ساعة ثم لا يتعارفون بعد تلك الساعة

rows.speaker: بعض الأخبار
rows.claim: Some reports say people flee those they know at the Resurrection for fear of unresolved grievances.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الأخبار: أن أهل القيامة يفرون من المعارف مخافة المظالم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In another explanation, people see and recognize one another before fleeing; the pronoun refers to disbelievers and its object to their relatives.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: { يبصرونهم } يبصر بعضهم بعضا فيتعارفون ثم يفر بعضهم من بعض

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes the subject as believers whom God shows the disbelievers at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: المعنى يبصر الله المؤمنين الكفار في يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes the subject as followers in Hell whom God shows the leaders who misled them in worldly life.
rows.anchor: ابن زيد: المعنى يبصر الله الكفار في النار الذين أضلوهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the oppressed will see their oppressor and the murdered person his killer.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه يبصر المظلوم ظالمه والمقتول قاتله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view refers the pronoun to angels, who know people's states and lead each group to its fitting destination.
rows.anchor: وقيل «يبصرونهم» يرجع إلى الملائكة أي يعرفون أحوال الناس فيسوقون كل فريق إلى ما يليق بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence is complete at يبصرونهم.
rows.anchor: وتم الكلام عند قوله: { يبصرونهم }. ثم قال: { يود المجرم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-mujrim means the disbeliever, who wishes to ransom himself from that day's punishment with his dearest worldly kin but cannot.
rows.anchor: { يود المجرم } أي يتمنى الكافر. { لو يفتدي من عذاب يومئذ } يعني من عذاب جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The listed loved ones are his sons, wife, brother, and faction; his fasila is his clan.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكرهم فقال: { ببنيه. وصاحبته } وزوجته. { وأخيه. وفصيلته } أي عشيرته

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن زيد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explain the fasila as the clan that supports a man.
rows.anchor: تنصره قاله مجاهد وابن زيد

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says the fasila is a man's mother, who raises him; al-Mawardi transmits this from him through Ashhab.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: أمه التي تربيه. حكاه الماوردي ورواه عنه أشهب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines the fasila as a kin group below the tribe.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الفصيلة دون القبيلة

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab defines a man's fasila as his nearest fathers.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب: هم آباؤه الأدنون

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says fasila means a piece of the body, a smaller unit than a tribe.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: الفصيلة القطعة من أعضاء الجسد، وهي دون القبيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man's ʿitra is called his fasila by analogy with a part of his body.
rows.anchor: وسميت عترة الرجل فصيلته تشبيها بالبعض منه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For an endowment or bequest to one's fasila, the general reading means the clan, while the narrow reading means nearest forefathers; the general sense is more common in speech.
rows.anchor: وهنا مسألة، وهي: إذا حبس على فصيلته أو أوصى لها فمن ادعى العموم حمله على العشيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾwīhi means to gather him in and protect him from fear if he is afraid.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: «تؤويه» تضمه وتؤمنه من خوف إن كان به.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The criminal would wish to offer everyone on earth as ransom to free himself.
rows.anchor: أي ويود لوفدي بهم لافتدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted phrase is required: that ransom would save him, as in the omitted object in 6:121.
rows.anchor: فلا بد من هذا الإضمار، كقوله: { وإنه لفسق } أي وإن أكله لفسق.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another analysis treats the wish as requiring a جواب with fa, as in 68:9, with ثم ينجيه supplying the answer: the ransom would save him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «يود المجرم» يقتضي جوابا بالفاء كقوله: { ودوا لو تدهن فيدهنون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla can mean indeed, completing the preceding sentence at ينجيه, or no, completing the sentence there to deny that ransom can save him.
rows.anchor: وهي هنا تحتمل الأمرين فإذا كانت بمعنى حقا كان تمام الكلام «ينجيه». وإذا كانت بمعنى لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laza is Hell, whose flames blaze; the wording is linked to the fire that blazes in 92:14.
rows.anchor: أي هي جهنم أي تتلظى نيرانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is derived from talazzī: iltizāʾ is a fire's ignition, and talazzī is its blazing.
rows.anchor: واشتقاق لظي من التلظي. والتظاء النار التهابها، وتلظيها تلهبها.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another etymology derives the name from an original laẓẓ, denoting the duration of its punishment, with one emphatic consonant changed to a long alif.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان أصلها «لظظ» أي مادامت لدوام عذابها فقلبت إحدى الظائين ألفا فبقيت لظى.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies Laza as the second level among the levels of Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي الدركة الثانية من طبقات جهنم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laza is a definite feminine proper name and therefore does not decline.
rows.anchor: وهي اسم مؤنث معرفة فلا ينصرف.

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي والأعمش
rows.claim: These reciters read nazzāʿa with nominative inflection; the source specifies Abu Bakr's transmission from Asim.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة ونافع وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر عنه والأعمش وأبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي «نزاعة» بالرفع.

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو عن عاصم
rows.claim: A transmission from Abu Amr from Asim reads nazzāʿa in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو عمرو عن عاصم «نزاعة» بالنصب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the nominative reading, Laza is inna's predicate and nazzāʿa has an omitted subject, hiya; stopping at Laza is then sound.
rows.anchor: أحدها أن تجعل «لظى» خبر «إن» وترفع «نزاعة» بإضمار هي فمن هذا الوجه يحسن الوقف على «لظى».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second nominative analysis makes both Laza and nazzāʿa predicates of inna.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثاني أن تكون «لظى» و «نزاعة» خبران لإن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third nominative analysis makes nazzāʿa an appositive to Laza, which is inna's predicate.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثالث أن تكون «نزاعة» بدلا من «لظى» و «لظى» خبر «إن».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth nominative analysis makes Laza appositive to inna's noun and nazzāʿa its predicate.
rows.anchor: والوجه الرابع أن تكون «لظى» بدلا من اسم «إن» و «نزاعة» خبر «إن».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth nominative analysis treats inna's pronoun as the pronoun of the affair, with Laza as subject and nazzāʿa as predicate.
rows.anchor: والوجه الخامس أن يكون الضمير في «إنها» للقصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the accusative reading, one may stop at Laza and make nazzāʿa a detached accusative because an indefinite follows a definite.
rows.anchor: ومن نصب «نزاعة» حسن له أن يقف على «لظى» وينصب «نزاعة» على القطع من «لظى» إذ كانت نكرة متصلة بمعرفة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative can also be an emphatic circumstantial accusative, compared with the example cited from 2:19.
rows.anchor: ويجوز نصبها على الحال المؤكدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It can describe Hell as blazing while stripping flesh; its governing factor is the implied sense of blazing.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تنصب على معنى أنها تتلظى نزاعة أي في حال نزعها للشوى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another accusative analysis makes it a circumstantial phrase describing those who deny what Hell reports.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون حالا على أنه حال للمكذبين بخبرها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further accusative analysis treats it as detached, as in the example of passing by Zayd the intelligent, excellent man.
rows.anchor: ويجوز نصبها على القطع كما تقول: مررت بزيد العاقل الفاضل

rows.speaker: قتيلة
rows.claim: Qutayla's line uses shawātuhu for the skin of the head covered with gray hair.
rows.anchor: قالت قتيلة ماله قد جللت شيبا شواته

rows.speaker: شاعر آخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet likewise refers to the scalp and its gray hair; qutayr means gray hair.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: لأصبحت هدتك الحوادث هدة لها فشواة الرأس باد قتيرها

rows.speaker: الصحاح
rows.claim: Al-Sihah defines shawā as the plural of shawāt, the skin of the head.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: «والشوى: جمع شواة وهي جلدة الرأس».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shawā can mean a person's hands, feet, head, or any part that is not a vital target; to strike without killing is to ashwā him.
rows.anchor: والشوى: اليدان والرجلان والرأس من الآدميين، وكل ما ليس مقتلا.

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: The Hudhali poet's phrase lā shawā lahā describes speech that does not merely wound but kills.
rows.anchor: يقال: رماه فأشواه إذا لم يصب المقتل. قال الهذلي: فإن من القول التي لا شوى لها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd says Abu al-Khattab al-Akhfash first recited the line to Abu Amr with sarātuhu, meaning its sides, then admitted the correct word was shawātuhu.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: أنشدها أبو الخطاب الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a horse, shawā means its legs: horses are described by full limbs, while their cheeks and faces are praised for being fine.
rows.anchor: وشوى الفرس: قوائمه لأنه يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shawā can also mean inferior property.
rows.anchor: والشوى: رذال المال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shawā can also mean something slight or insignificant.
rows.anchor: والشوى: هو الشيء الهين اليسير.

rows.speaker: ثابت البناني والحسن
rows.claim: Thabit al-Bunani and al-Hasan say that shawā means the beauties of the face.
rows.anchor: وقال ثابت البناني والحسن: { نزاعة للشوى } أي لمكارم وجهه.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya takes shawā to mean the fine features of the face.
rows.anchor: أبو العالية: لمحاسن وجهه.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says it means the noble parts of a person's creation and the extremities.
rows.anchor: قتادة: لمكارم خلقته وأطرافه.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says Hell strips flesh and skin from the bone until nothing remains.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: تفري اللحم والجلد عن العظم حتى لا تترك منه شيئا.

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi identifies shawā as the joints.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: هي المفاصل.

rows.speaker: بعض الأئمة
rows.claim: Some authorities say shawā means the legs and skins.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الأئمة: هي القوائم والجلود.

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays's description of a horse as ʿabl al-shawā uses shawā for its limbs.
rows.anchor: قال امرؤ القيس: سليم الشظى عبل الشوى شنج النسا

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih defines shawā as the ends of the hands and feet; a poet uses it for an animal's extremities.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: أطراف اليدين والرجلين.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also says shawā means the heads.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن أيضا: الشوى الهام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laza calls those who turned away from God's obedience and faith in worldly life, summoning them as disbelievers and polytheists.
rows.anchor: أي تدعو لظى من أدبر في الدنيا عن طاعة الله وتولى عن الإيمان.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says it calls disbelievers and hypocrites by name in a clear voice, then snatches them as a bird picks up grain.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: تدعو الكافرين والمنافقين بأسمائهم بلسان فصيح

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab interprets tadʿū as destroy, citing the Arab expression daʿāka Allāh for may God destroy you.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب: «تدعو» أي تهلك. تقول العرب: دعاك الله أي أهلكك الله.

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says the call is not an invitation to come, but its power to summon them into torment.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: إنه ليس كالدعاء «تعالوا» ولكن دعوتها إياهم تمكنها من تعذيبهم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the keepers of Hell are the callers, with their call attributed to Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الداعي خزنة جهنم أضيف دعاؤهم إليها.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the wording as a figure: the fate of those who turned away is Hell, so it is as though Hell called them.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو ضرب مثل أي إن مصير من أدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is told to tell his community that God revealed through Gabriel that a group of jinn listened; Ibn Abbas and others say he had not known before the revelation.
rows.anchor: أي قل يا محمد لأمتك: أوحى الله إلي على لسان جبريل

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads aḥiya, preserving the original form; the source compares the change of wāw to hamza with 77:11.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة «أحي» على الأصل يقال: أوحى إليه ووحى، فقلبت الواو همزة ومنه قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing a wāw to hamza is generally permitted when the wāw bears ḍamma; al-Mazini extends the allowance to kasra and gives examples.
rows.anchor: وهو من القلب المطلق جوازه في كل واو مضمومة. وقد أطلقه المازني في المكسورة أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent wording, especially istamaʿa, indicates that the Prophet did not see the jinn; the source links this to 46:29.
rows.anchor: فظاهر القرآن يدل على أنه لم يرهم لقوله تعالى: { استمع }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet neither recited to the jinn nor saw them: a group at Nakhlah heard his dawn recitation and returned to warn their people.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم والترمذي عن ابن عباس قال: ما قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على الجن وما رآهم،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that when the jinn saw the Prophet praying with his companions and they followed his prostration, they marveled at their obedience and said they nearly crowded around him.
rows.anchor: رواه الترمذي عن ابن عباس قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi grades the preceding report hasan sahih; it shows the Prophet did not see the jinn, though they attended and heard his recitation.
rows.anchor: قال: هذا حديث حسن صحيح ففي هذا الحديث دليل على أنه عليه السلام لم ير الجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn were with the devils when they searched for news because of the shooting stars; the ones pelted were jinn too.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على أن الجن كانوا مع الشياطين حين تجسسوا الخبر بسبب الشياطين لما رموا بالشهب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were called devils because shaytan denotes anyone rebellious and disobedient; the Quran also speaks of human and jinn devils in 6:112.
rows.anchor: فإن الشيطان كل متمرد وخارج عن طاعة الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report graded hasan sahih says jinn used to ascend to hear revelation and add nine false words to each true word; after the Prophet's mission they were barred, informed Iblis, and found the Prophet praying near Mecca.
rows.anchor: كان الجن يصعدون إلى السماء يستمعون إلى الوحي فإذا سمعوا الكلمة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the pelted jinn told Iblis, who had them bring soil from their lands, smelled it, identified Mecca, and dispatched a group.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية السدي: أنهم لما رموا أتوا إبليس فأخبروه بما كان من أمرهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says Iblis sent seven jinn, while another says nine, including Zawbaʿa.
rows.anchor: فبعث نفرا من الجن، قيل: كانوا سبعة. وقيل: تسعة منهم زوبعة.

rows.speaker: عاصم عن زر
rows.claim: Asim from Zirr reports that Zawbaʿa and his companions came to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وروى عاصم عن زر قال: قدم رهط زوبعة وأصحابه على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم.

rows.speaker: الثمالي
rows.claim: Al-Thumali says he heard that they were Banu al-Shaysaban, the most numerous and formidable jinn, who formed the main body of Iblis's troops.
rows.anchor: وقال الثمالي: بلغني أنهم من بني الشيصبان، وهم أكثر الجن عددا

rows.speaker: عاصم عن زر
rows.claim: Another report from Asim and Zirr says there were seven: three from Harran and four from Nasibin.
rows.anchor: وروي أيضا عاصم عن زر: أنهم كانوا سبعة نفر ثلاثة من أهل حران وأربعة من أهل نصيبين.

rows.speaker: جويبر عن الضحاك
rows.claim: Juwaybir reports from al-Dahhak that nine were from Nasibin, a town in Yemen distinct from the Iraqi town of that name.
rows.anchor: وحكي جويبر عن الضحاك: أنهم كانوا تسعة من أهل نصيبين قرية باليمن غير التي بالعراق.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account distinguishes the jinn who came to Mecca as from Nasibin and those who came to Nakhlah as from Nineveh.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الجن الذين أتوا مكة جن نصيبين، والذين أتوه بنخلة جن نينوى.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies the surah the Prophet was reciting as the opening of al-ʿAlaq, completed in the following passage.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: والسورة التي كان يقرؤها رسول الله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says the Prophet was reciting Read in the name of your Lord (96:1); the jinn's names were already given in al-Ahqaf and need not be repeated.
rows.anchor: اقرأ باسم ربك [العلق: 1] وقد مضى

rows.speaker: عامر الشعبي عن علقمة عن ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi asked Alqama about Ibn Masud's encounter with the jinn. Ibn Masud said he was not with the Prophet that night; later the Prophet told him a jinn caller had taken him to recite, showed him their traces and fires, and the jinn asked for food and fodder, which he supplied with a warning against using bones or dung for cleansing.
rows.anchor: روى عامر الشعبي قال: سألت علقمة هل كان ابن مسعود شهد مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ليلة الجن؟

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says Ibn Masud's account is more authoritative than Ibn Abbas's because Ibn Masud witnessed the event, whereas Ibn Abbas heard about it; eyewitnessing is not like report.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وابن مسعود أعرف من ابن عباس لأنه شاهده وابن عباس سمعه وليس الخبر كالمعاينة.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reconciliation says the jinn came twice: first at Mecca in Ibn Masud's account, then at Nakhlah in Ibn Abbas's.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن الجن أتوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم دفعتين: إحداهما بمكة وهي التي ذكرها ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi reconciles the reports by saying Ibn Abbas describes the first hearing, when the Prophet neither recited to nor saw them, and Ibn Masud describes a later summons when he recited to them.
rows.anchor: قال البيهقي: الذي حكاه عبد الله بن عباس إنما هو في أول ما سمعت الجن قراءة النبي

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi says sound hadiths show Ibn Masud was not with the Prophet on the night of the jinn, but went with him later to see their traces and fires; other routes place him there.
rows.anchor: قال البيهقي: والأحاديث الصحاح تدل على أن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In Ibn Masud's report, the Prophet asks who will accompany him to recite to the jinn; Ibn Masud volunteers, waits within a marked boundary, and is told they listened and returned as warners. They request provisions, receive bones and dung, and Muslims are forbidden to use them for cleansing.
rows.anchor: أمرت أن أتلوا القرآن على الجن فمن يذهب معي؟» فسكتوا، ثم قال الثانية

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says the group numbered twelve thousand and came from the Island of Mosul.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: وكانوا اثني عشر ألفا من جزيرة الموصل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report describes jinn like men of Zutt with magpie-like faces; a tree came at the Prophet's call, testified to his prophethood, then returned to its place.
rows.anchor: فأتاه نفر منهم فقال أصحابنا كأنهم رجال الزط وكأن وجوههم المكاكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the Prophet rested his head on Ibn Masud's stone, awoke and asked for water to perform ablution; he used date water from Ibn Masud's vessel.
rows.anchor: أنه عليه السلام لما فرغ وضع رأسه على حجر ابن مسعود فرقد ثم استيقظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source says the discussion of water and cleansing materials was already covered in al-Hijr and al-Tawbah.
rows.anchor: الثالثة قد مضى الكلام في الماء

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says jinn descend from Iblis and humans from Adam; each kind includes believers and unbelievers, sharing in reward and punishment, with believers God's allies and unbelievers devils.
rows.anchor: فروى إسماعيل عن الحسن البصري: أن الجن ولد إبليس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says jinn descend from al-Jann, not the devils; they include believers and unbelievers, while devils descend from Iblis and die only with him.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس: أن الجن هم ولد الجان وليسوا بشياطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether believing jinn enter Paradise depends on their origin: if from al-Jann, they enter through faith; if from Iblis, two views follow.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا في دخول مؤمني الجن الجنة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: If jinn descend from Iblis, al-Hasan's view is that believing jinn nevertheless enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: ومن قال: إنهم من ذرية إبليس فلهم فيه قولان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid's reported view is that believing jinn descended from Iblis do not enter Paradise, though they are kept from Hell.
rows.anchor: الثاني وهو رواية مجاهد لا يدخلونها وإن صرفوا عن النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source points to 55:56 as establishing that jinn enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: لم يطمثهن إنس قبلهم ولا جان [الرحمن: 56] بيان أنهم يدخلونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn's request for provisions, especially bones, establishes that they eat and drink.
rows.anchor: دليل على أنهم يأكلون ويطعمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some unbelieving physicians and philosophers deny jinn as simple substances unable to eat; the Quran and Sunna refute them, since no created being is simple and only God is truly one.
rows.anchor: وقد أنكر جماعة من كفرة الأطباء والفلاسفة الجن، وقالوا: إنهم بسائط، ولا يصح طعامهم اجتراء على الله وافتراء، والقرآن والسنة ترد عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No created being is simple: only God is truly one, while all other beings are composite.
rows.anchor: وليس في المخلوقات بسيط مركب مزدوج، إنما الواحد الواحد سبحانه، وغيره مركب وليس بواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet could see jinn in their own forms just as he could see angels.
rows.anchor: وليس يمتنع أن يراهم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في صورهم كما يرى الملائكة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn most often appear to people as snakes.
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما يتصورون لنا في صور الحيات

rows.speaker: الموطأ
rows.claim: A report in al-Muwattaʾ tells of a recently married man who found a huge snake coiled on his bed and killed it with a spear.
rows.anchor: فإذا حية عظيمة منطوية على الفراش

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A sahih report says houses have resident jinn: warn a snake three times, then kill it if it remains; the Prophet called it an unbeliever and ordered its burial.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح أنه عليه السلام قال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some restrict the warning rule to Medina, citing a sahih report that jinn in Medina had accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب قوم إلى أن ذلك مخصوص بالمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects a Medina-only restriction: the report's rationale is the snakes' Islam, not Medina's sanctity, and that rationale applies elsewhere too.
rows.anchor: قلنا: هذا يدل على أن غيرها من البيوت مثلها لأنه لم يعلل بحرمة المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that the encountered jinn were from the island and a general prohibition on killing house snakes support applying the rule beyond Medina.
rows.anchor: وهذا بين يعضده قوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of wondrous Quran is the eloquence of its language.
rows.anchor: { فقالوا إنا سمعنا قرآنا عجبا } أي في فصاحة كلامه.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view finds its wonder in the eloquence of its exhortations.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عجبا في بلاغة مواعظه.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says it is wondrous for the greatness of its blessing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عجبا في عظم بركته.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation calls it mighty and without equal.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قرآنا عزيزا لا يوجد مثله.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes wondrous to mean great.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعنون عظيما.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-rushd means sound and right courses of action.
rows.anchor: { يهدي إلى الرشد } أي إلى مراشد الأمور.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says it guides to knowledge of God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إلى معرفة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yahdī is an adjective here, meaning hādiyan, guiding.
rows.anchor: في موضع الصفة أي هاديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their belief means they were guided by the Quran and affirmed that it came from God.
rows.anchor: أي فاهتدينا به وصدقنا أنه من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that they will not return to Iblis or obey him, since he had sent them to investigate the news.
rows.anchor: أي لا نرجع إلى إبليس ولا نطيعه لأنه الذي كان بعثهم ليأتوه بالخبر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they will take no other deity alongside God, who alone possesses lordship.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا نتخذ مع الله إلها آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn's discernment throws into relief the Quraysh polytheists' failure to recognize what reflection on the Quran showed the jinn.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تعجيب المؤمنين بذهاب مشركي قريش عما أدركته الجن بتدبرها القرآن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unstated object of listened is the Prophet, supplied by the context; the jinn learned his recitation was God's speech.
rows.anchor: أي استمعوا إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فعلموا أن ما يقرؤه كلام الله.

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil defines nafar as a group of three to ten.
rows.anchor: والنفر الرهط قال الخليل: ما بين ثلاثة إلى عشرة.

rows.speaker: عيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: Isa al-Thaqafi reads rashad with fatḥa on both the ra and shin.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى الثقفي «يهدي إلى الرشد» بفتح الراء والشين.

rows.speaker: علقمة ويحيى والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وابن عامر وخلف وحفص والسلمي
rows.claim: These reciters read the hamza with fatḥa at twelve listed clauses across the surah, including wa-annahu taʿālā jaddu rabbinā.
rows.anchor: كان علقمة ويحيى والأعمش وحمزة والكسائي وابن عامر وخلف وحفص والسلمي ينصبون «أن» في جميع السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatḥa readings can be coordinated with the clause that a group of jinn listened; the opening clause itself must be fatḥa as the complement of ūḥiya.
rows.anchor: عطفا على قوله: { أنه استمع نفر }

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parsing coordinates it with the pronoun in āmannā bihi, permitted despite the pronoun's genitive because anna recurs after a long stretch of prepositions.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو محمول على الهاء في «آمنا به» أي وب«أنه تعالى جد ربنا» وجاز ذلك وهو مضمر مجرور لكثرة حرف الجار مع «أن».

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A paraphrase of that reading is: we believed that our Lord's majesty is exalted.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى أي وصدقنا أنه جد ربنا.

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers use kasra throughout; al-Qurtubi calls this correct and follows Abu Ubayda and Abu Hatim, who coordinate the clauses with the jinn's speech after فقالوا إنا سمعنا.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون كلها بالكسر وهو الصواب، واختاره أبو عبيدة وأبو حاتم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba open the hamza at three clauses because they take them as revelation, and read the rest with kasra as the jinn's speech.
rows.anchor: وأما أبو جعفر وشيبة فإنهما فتحا ثلاثة مواضع وهي قوله تعالى: { وأنه تعالى جد ربنا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All reciters agree on fatḥa in wa-an law istaqāmū.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في فتح همزة { أنه استمع نفر من الجن }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All reciters agree on fatḥa in wa-anna al-masājida lillāh; the source also lists wa-an qad ablaghū among the unanimous fatḥa readings.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في فتح همزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All reciters agree that the hamza is kasra after speech, as in fa-qālū innā samiʿnā, qāla innamā adʿū rabbī, and qul innī lā adrī.
rows.anchor: وكذلك لا خلاق في كسرها ما بعد القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza is fatḥa; one parsing connects the clause to قل أوحي إلي, while al-Khalil reads it as because the mosques belong to God.
rows.anchor: بالفتح، قيل: هو مردود إلى قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first explanation, mosques are the houses that religious communities build for worship.
rows.anchor: والمراد البيوت التي تبنيها أهل الملل للعبادة.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the jinn asked how they could come to mosques and join the prayer while far away; the verse says they were built for remembrance and obedience to God.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: قالت الجن كيف لنا أن نأتي المساجد ونشهد معك الصلاة ونحن ناءون عنك؟

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan takes mosques to mean every place on earth, since the whole earth was made a place of prostration for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: أراد بها كل البقاع لأن الأرض كلها مسجد للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Prophetic reports say to pray wherever one is and that wherever one prays is a mosque.
rows.anchor:
للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، يقول:
" أينما كنتم فصلوا "
" فأينما صليتم فهو مسجد "

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A sahih report says the earth was made a mosque and a means of purification for the Prophet.
rows.anchor:
وفي الصحيح:
" وجعلت لي الأرض مسجدا وطهورا "

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب وطلق بن حبيب
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib and Talq ibn Habib identify the mosques as the limbs used in prostration, which must not be used to prostrate to other than God, their giver.
rows.anchor: أراد بالمساجد الأعضاء التي يسجد عليها العبد

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says the limbs commanded to prostrate should not be humbled before anyone but their Creator.
rows.anchor: مساجدك: أعضاؤك التي أمرت أن تسجد عليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports the Prophet was commanded to prostrate on seven bones: the forehead, nose, hands, knees, and toes.
rows.anchor:
وفي الصحيح عن ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:
" أمرت أن أسجد على سبعة أعظم: الجبهة

rows.speaker: العباس
rows.claim: Al-Abbas reports the Prophet said that when a servant prostrates, seven joints prostrate with him.
rows.anchor:
وقال العباس قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:
" إذا سجد العبد سجد معه سبعة آراب "

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also says mosques means the prayers, since prostration belongs to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المساجد هي الصلوات أي لأن السجود لله. قاله الحسن أيضا.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: If mosques means places, the singular is masjid with kasra on the jim, though al-Farraʾ also reports a form with fatḥa.
rows.anchor: فإن جعلت المساجد المواضع فواحدها مسجد بكسر الجيم، ويقال بالفتح حكاه الفراء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If mosques means bodily limbs, the singular masjad has fatḥa on the jim.
rows.anchor: وإن جعلتها الأعضاء لواحدها مسجد بفتح الجيم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another analysis treats masājid as the plural of masjid meaning prostration, a verbal noun like madrab for traveling in search of livelihood.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو جمع مسجد وهو السجود

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the mosques are Mecca, the direction of prayer, called mosques because everyone prostrates toward it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: المساجد هنا مكة التي هي القبلة وسميت مكة المساجد لأن كل أحد يسجد إليها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi prefers the first explanation, that mosques are houses of worship, and says it is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول أظهر هذه الأقوال إن شاء الله، وهو مروي عن ابن عباس رحمه الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive attribution to God expresses honor and distinction; the sacred House is then singled out.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { لله } إضافة تشريف وتكريم، ثم خص بالذكر منها البيت العتيق فقال:
